question: Under Section 83.57, F.S., a landlord or tenant seeking to terminate a year-to-year residential tenancy with no specific term must give written notice of not less than:
choice_a: 60 days prior to the end of the annual period
choice_b: 15 days prior to the end of the annual period
choice_c: 7 days prior to the end of the annual period
choice_d: There is no notice requirement for year-to-year tenancies
explanation: Section 83.57, F.S., requires not less than 60 days' written notice prior to the end of the annual period to terminate a year-to-year tenancy with no specific duration -- the longest of the statutory periodic-tenancy notice periods, reflecting the longer rental cycle involved.
source_note: Section 83.57, F.S. (termination of tenancy without specific term -- year-to-year)

question: Under Section 83.57, F.S., a landlord or tenant seeking to terminate a month-to-month residential tenancy with no specific term must give written notice of not less than:
choice_a: 30 days prior to the end of the monthly period
choice_b: 60 days prior to the end of the monthly period
choice_c: 5 days prior to the end of the monthly period
choice_d: No written notice is required for a month-to-month tenancy
explanation: Section 83.57, F.S., requires not less than 30 days' written notice prior to the end of the monthly period to terminate a month-to-month tenancy with no specific term -- distinct from the 3-day pay-or-vacate notice used for nonpayment of rent under Section 83.56(3), F.S.
source_note: Section 83.57, F.S. (termination of tenancy without specific term -- month-to-month)

question: Under Section 83.57, F.S., a landlord or tenant seeking to terminate a week-to-week residential tenancy with no specific term must give written notice of not less than:
choice_a: 7 days prior to the end of the weekly period
choice_b: 30 days prior to the end of the weekly period
choice_c: 60 days prior to the end of the weekly period
choice_d: 1 day prior to the end of the weekly period
explanation: Section 83.57, F.S., requires not less than 7 days' written notice prior to the end of the weekly period to terminate a week-to-week tenancy with no specific term -- the shortest of the four periodic-tenancy notice periods.
source_note: Section 83.57, F.S. (termination of tenancy without specific term -- week-to-week)

question: Under Section 83.57, F.S., a landlord or tenant seeking to terminate a quarter-to-quarter residential tenancy with no specific term must give written notice of not less than:
choice_a: 30 days prior to the end of the quarterly period
choice_b: 90 days prior to the end of the quarterly period
choice_c: 60 days prior to the end of the quarterly period
choice_d: 14 days prior to the end of the quarterly period
explanation: Section 83.57, F.S., requires not less than 30 days' written notice prior to the end of the quarterly period to terminate a quarter-to-quarter tenancy with no specific term -- the same 30-day period required for a month-to-month tenancy, even though the underlying rental period is longer.
source_note: Section 83.57, F.S. (termination of tenancy without specific term -- quarter-to-quarter)

question: Under Section 83.53, F.S., when a landlord needs to enter a tenant's dwelling unit to make repairs (not an emergency), the landlord must generally give the tenant notice of the landlord's intent to enter of at least:
choice_a: 24 hours, and may only enter between 7:30 a.m. and 8:00 p.m.
choice_b: 1 hour, at any time of day or night
choice_c: 7 days, in writing only
choice_d: No notice is required for repair visits
explanation: Section 83.53, F.S., requires a landlord to give the tenant notice of at least 24 hours before entering to make repairs, and entry for that purpose is restricted to reasonable hours between 7:30 a.m. and 8:00 p.m.
source_note: Section 83.53, F.S. (landlord's access to dwelling unit -- notice and hours for repairs)

question: Under Section 83.53, F.S., a landlord may enter a tenant's dwelling unit without advance notice and without the tenant's consent when:
choice_a: An emergency exists
choice_b: The landlord simply wants to check on general upkeep, with no notice ever required for any purpose
choice_c: The tenant is more than one day late on rent
choice_d: A prospective buyer asks to see the unit at any hour
explanation: Section 83.53, F.S., permits a landlord to enter the dwelling unit without advance notice or tenant consent in case of an emergency -- one of the narrow exceptions to the statute's general advance-notice requirement for landlord access.
source_note: Section 83.53, F.S. (landlord's access to dwelling unit -- emergency entry)

question: Under Section 83.53, F.S., a landlord may also enter a tenant's dwelling unit without notice when the tenant has been absent from the premises for a continuous period equal to:
choice_a: One-half the time for periodic rental payments, unless the tenant has notified the landlord of an intended absence and rent is current
choice_b: Any single day, regardless of rent status
choice_c: One full calendar year
choice_d: This is never permitted under Florida law, regardless of the length of the tenant's absence
explanation: Section 83.53, F.S., allows a landlord to enter without notice if the tenant is absent from the premises for a period equal to one-half the time for periodic rental payments -- unless the tenant has notified the landlord of an intended absence and the rent is current, in which case this entry right does not apply.
source_note: Section 83.53, F.S. (landlord's access to dwelling unit -- tenant absence)

question: Under Section 83.53, F.S., a property manager exercising the landlord's statutory right of entry to a tenant's dwelling unit must:
choice_a: Not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant
choice_b: Enter as frequently as desired for any reason, with no limitation whatsoever
choice_c: Only be permitted to enter if the tenant is present and personally lets the manager in each time
choice_d: Obtain a court order before every single entry, even for routine repairs
explanation: Section 83.53, F.S., expressly provides that the landlord (or property manager acting on the landlord's behalf) shall not abuse the right of access to the dwelling unit or use it to harass the tenant, even where notice has been properly given.
source_note: Section 83.53, F.S. (landlord's access to dwelling unit -- no abuse or harassment)

question: Under Section 83.51(2), F.S., a landlord of a building containing three or more residential dwelling units must generally provide reasonable, ongoing provisions for which of the following?
choice_a: Extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs; locks and keys; clean common areas; garbage removal; and functioning heat, running water, and hot water
choice_b: Only interior painting, with no other maintenance obligation
choice_c: Free cable television service to every unit
choice_d: A dedicated on-site gym facility
explanation: Section 83.51(2), F.S., requires landlords of buildings with three or more dwelling units to provide reasonable, ongoing provisions for pest extermination (rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs), locks and keys, clean and safe common areas, garbage removal and receptacles, and functioning heat, running water, and hot water.
source_note: Section 83.51(2), F.S. (landlord's obligation to maintain premises -- buildings of 3+ units)

question: Under Section 83.51(2), F.S., a landlord's statutory maintenance obligations for pest control, locks, common areas, garbage removal, and utilities may be:
choice_a: Altered or modified in writing with respect to a single-family home or duplex, shifting certain responsibilities to the tenant
choice_b: Never modified under any circumstance, for any type of dwelling
choice_c: Waived orally at any time for any property type
choice_d: Delegated only to a licensed CAM, never to the tenant
explanation: Section 83.51(2), F.S., allows the landlord's statutory maintenance obligations to be altered or modified by written agreement specifically with respect to a single-family home or duplex, permitting the parties to shift certain maintenance responsibilities to the tenant for those property types.
source_note: Section 83.51(2), F.S. (maintenance obligations may be modified in writing for single-family homes/duplexes)

question: Under Section 83.51, F.S., a landlord renting out a single-family home or duplex must, at the commencement of the tenancy, generally ensure the unit has:
choice_a: Working smoke detection devices
choice_b: A fully stocked first-aid kit
choice_c: A dedicated fire extinguisher in every room
choice_d: No specific safety equipment is required by statute
explanation: Section 83.51, F.S., requires a landlord of a single-family home or duplex to install working smoke detection devices at the commencement of the tenancy, a specific life-safety requirement distinct from the general habitability and maintenance duties.
source_note: Section 83.51, F.S. (smoke detection devices -- single-family homes and duplexes)

question: Under Section 83.51, F.S., a landlord is generally NOT responsible for maintaining or repairing a condition in the dwelling unit that was:
choice_a: Created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant
choice_b: Present at the start of the original lease term, regardless of cause
choice_c: Caused by ordinary wear and tear from normal use
choice_d: Disclosed to the landlord in writing before the tenant moved in
explanation: Section 83.51, F.S., relieves the landlord of responsibility for conditions created or caused by the tenant's own negligent or wrongful act or omission -- the landlord's maintenance duty applies to conditions arising in the ordinary course, not damage the tenant itself caused.
source_note: Section 83.51, F.S. (no landlord liability for tenant-caused conditions)

question: Under Section 83.56(1), F.S., if a landlord's material noncompliance with its maintenance duties renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates as a result, the tenant:
choice_a: Shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable
choice_b: Remains fully liable for rent for the entire remaining lease term regardless of habitability
choice_c: Forfeits the security deposit automatically
choice_d: Must continue paying rent but may sue only after the lease naturally expires
explanation: Section 83.56(1)(a), F.S., provides that when the landlord's failure to comply renders the unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant is not liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable.
source_note: Section 83.56(1)(a), F.S. (rent abatement for untenantable premises)

question: Under Section 83.56(1), F.S., if a landlord's noncompliance does NOT render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the appropriate remedy is generally that:
choice_a: The rent for the period of noncompliance is reduced by an amount proportional to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance
choice_b: The tenant may withhold 100% of rent regardless of the severity of the issue
choice_c: The lease automatically terminates with no further landlord liability
choice_d: No remedy is available if the tenant chooses to stay in the unit
explanation: Section 83.56(1)(b), F.S., provides that when the landlord's noncompliance does not render the unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance is reduced in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance -- a partial abatement rather than full withholding.
source_note: Section 83.56(1)(b), F.S. (proportional rent reduction for partial noncompliance)

question: Under Section 83.56(2), F.S., when a tenant commits a curable lease violation (other than nonpayment of rent), the landlord must generally deliver a written notice specifying the noncompliance and give the tenant an opportunity to cure of:
choice_a: 7 days from delivery of the written notice
choice_b: 60 days from delivery of the written notice
choice_c: 24 hours from delivery of the written notice
choice_d: There is no cure period; the landlord may terminate immediately for any violation
explanation: Section 83.56(2)(a), F.S., requires the landlord to deliver written notice specifying a curable noncompliance and to give the tenant 7 days from delivery of that notice to correct the violation before the landlord may terminate the rental agreement on that basis.
source_note: Section 83.56(2)(a), F.S. (tenant's 7-day cure period for curable noncompliance)

question: Under Section 83.56(2), F.S., if a tenant's same type of lease noncompliance recurs within 12 months after the landlord's prior written notice on that issue, the landlord generally:
choice_a: May commence an eviction action without delivering another 7-day cure notice for the repeat violation
choice_b: Must always give a fresh 7-day cure notice for every occurrence, no matter how many times it recurs
choice_c: Loses the right to evict entirely after giving one prior warning
choice_d: Must wait a full additional 12 months before taking any action
explanation: Section 83.56(2)(b), F.S., provides that if the same type of noncompliance recurs within 12 months of a prior written notice, the landlord may proceed with an eviction action without delivering a further cure notice, since the tenant already had the earlier opportunity to correct the behavior.
source_note: Section 83.56(2)(b), F.S. (repeat noncompliance within 12 months -- no further notice required)

question: Under Section 83.49(2), F.S., separate from the 30-day notice required when a landlord later intends to make a claim against a security deposit, a landlord must also give the tenant an initial written notice -- either in the lease or within 30 days after receipt of advance rent or a security deposit -- disclosing:
choice_a: The name and address of the depository where the funds are held (or that a surety bond has been posted), and whether the funds bear interest
choice_b: The landlord's personal social security number
choice_c: The tenant's credit score at move-in
choice_d: Nothing; no initial disclosure of any kind is ever required
explanation: Section 83.49(2), F.S., requires a landlord to give the tenant written notice -- in the lease itself or within 30 days after receiving advance rent or a security deposit -- disclosing the name and address of the depository holding the funds (or that a surety bond was posted) and whether the funds are interest-bearing. This initial disclosure notice is distinct from the later 30-day notice of intent to impose a claim after the tenant vacates.
source_note: Section 83.49(2), F.S. (initial deposit disclosure notice, distinct from the claim notice)

question: Under Section 83.49(2), F.S., a landlord's failure to provide the initial written notice disclosing where advance rent or a security deposit is held:
choice_a: Is not a defense to the tenant's obligation to pay rent when due
choice_b: Automatically excuses the tenant from paying rent for the remainder of the lease
choice_c: Automatically terminates the lease in the tenant's favor
choice_d: Has no consequence whatsoever and creates no landlord obligation of any kind
explanation: Section 83.49(2), F.S., specifies that a landlord's failure to give the initial deposit disclosure notice is not a defense to the tenant's obligation to pay rent when due -- the tenant cannot withhold rent solely because this particular notice was not given, even though the landlord remains subject to the statute's other requirements.
source_note: Section 83.49(2), F.S. (failure to give initial notice is not a rent defense)

question: Under Section 83.49, F.S., which of the following is generally exempt from the statute's security deposit holding and notice requirements?
choice_a: Transient rentals by hotels or motels
choice_b: A single-family home rented on a standard annual lease
choice_c: A duplex managed by a licensed broker
choice_d: A high-rise condominium unit rented month-to-month
explanation: Section 83.49, F.S., exempts transient rentals by hotels or motels (which are governed by other statutory and regulatory frameworks for transient lodging) from its security deposit holding, notice, and claim procedures, which apply to ordinary residential tenancies.
source_note: Section 83.49, F.S. (exemption for hotel/motel transient rentals)

question: Under Section 83.43, F.S., the statutory definition of "advance rent" is money paid to the landlord to be applied to:
choice_a: Future rent payment periods, not including rent paid in advance for the current rent payment period
choice_b: Only the security deposit, since the two terms are legally identical
choice_c: The landlord's personal, unrelated expenses
choice_d: Attorney's fees in a future eviction only
explanation: Section 83.43, F.S., defines "advance rent" as moneys paid to the landlord to be applied to future rent payment periods, expressly excluding rent paid in advance for the current rent payment period -- a distinction relevant because advance rent, like a security deposit, is subject to Section 83.49's holding and notice requirements.
source_note: Section 83.43, F.S. (definition of "advance rent")

question: Under Section 83.43, F.S., the statutory definition of "security deposit" includes any moneys held by the landlord as security for performance of the rental agreement, including:
choice_a: Monetary damage to the landlord caused by the tenant's breach of the lease prior to its expiration
choice_b: Only funds explicitly labeled "security deposit" on the lease, regardless of their actual purpose
choice_c: The landlord's property insurance premium
choice_d: The real estate commission owed to the listing broker
explanation: Section 83.43, F.S., defines "security deposit" broadly to include any moneys held by the landlord as security for performance of the rental agreement, including, but not limited to, monetary damage to the landlord caused by the tenant's breach of the lease before its expiration -- regardless of what label the parties place on the funds.
source_note: Section 83.43, F.S. (definition of "security deposit")

question: Under Section 83.595, F.S., when a tenant breaches the rental agreement and vacates the premises before the lease term ends, one option available to the landlord is to:
choice_a: Treat the rental agreement as terminated and retake possession for the landlord's own account, which ends any further liability of the tenant for rent
choice_b: Automatically forfeit any right to retake possession of the unit
choice_c: Be legally required to leave the unit vacant for the rest of the original lease term
choice_d: Immediately sue the tenant criminally for breach of contract
explanation: Section 83.595, F.S., allows a landlord, upon a tenant's breach and vacating of the premises, to treat the rental agreement as terminated and retake possession for the landlord's own account -- an option that ends the tenant's further liability for rent going forward.
source_note: Section 83.595, F.S. (landlord's option -- terminate and retake for landlord's own account)

question: Under Section 83.595, F.S., instead of terminating the lease outright, a landlord may alternatively retake possession of the unit "for the account of the tenant" after the tenant's breach and vacating, meaning the landlord may:
choice_a: Hold the tenant liable for the difference between the rent due under the lease and what the landlord actually recovers by reletting the unit
choice_b: Never attempt to relet the unit under any circumstances
choice_c: Collect double rent from both the original tenant and any new tenant simultaneously
choice_d: Sue the tenant for the full remaining lease rent even after successfully reletting at the same rent
explanation: Section 83.595, F.S., allows a landlord to retake possession for the tenant's account, reletting the unit and holding the original tenant liable only for the difference (the shortfall) between the rent stipulated in the original lease and what the landlord actually recovers from the reletting.
source_note: Section 83.595, F.S. (landlord's option -- retake for the tenant's account)

question: Under Section 83.595, F.S., a landlord faced with a tenant who has breached the lease and vacated may also choose to:
choice_a: Stand by and do nothing, holding the tenant liable for the rent as it comes due for the remainder of the term
choice_b: Only ever be forced to immediately re-lease the property to the first available applicant
choice_c: Automatically waive the entire remaining balance of rent owed
choice_d: Be barred from recovering any rent at all once the tenant vacates
explanation: Section 83.595, F.S., permits a landlord, as one of several options, to stand by and do nothing -- neither terminating the lease nor reletting the unit -- and instead hold the tenant liable for rent as it becomes due under the original lease terms.
source_note: Section 83.595, F.S. (landlord's option -- stand by and collect rent as it comes due)

question: Under Section 83.595, F.S., a landlord and tenant may agree to liquidated damages or an early termination fee for a tenant's breach and early vacating, provided that the amount does not exceed:
choice_a: Two months' rent, and the tenant agreed to the provision by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement
choice_b: Twelve months' rent, with no separate signed addendum required
choice_c: There is no statutory cap of any kind on this type of fee
choice_d: One week's rent only, regardless of the lease's length
explanation: Section 83.595, F.S., allows landlords to charge liquidated damages or an early termination fee not exceeding two months' rent, but only where the tenant separately agreed to that specific provision by signing a distinct addendum to the rental agreement, rather than simply agreeing to the lease as a whole.
source_note: Section 83.595, F.S. (early termination fee -- two-month cap, separate signed addendum required)

question: Under Section 83.64, F.S., it is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent, decrease services, or bring or threaten an eviction action, when the landlord's primary motivation is:
choice_a: Retaliation against the tenant for exercising a legally protected right
choice_b: The tenant's simple failure to pay rent when due
choice_c: A documented, material lease violation unrelated to any protected activity
choice_d: The natural, scheduled expiration of the lease term
explanation: Section 83.64, F.S., prohibits a landlord from discriminatorily raising rent, cutting services, or bringing or threatening an eviction action primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant for exercising a legally protected right -- as opposed to acting for legitimate business or lease-compliance reasons.
source_note: Section 83.64, F.S. (retaliatory conduct -- general prohibition)

question: Under Section 83.64, F.S., a landlord's retaliatory conduct prohibition generally protects a tenant who has, among other things:
choice_a: Made a good-faith complaint to a governmental agency about a suspected building, housing, or health code violation
choice_b: Committed repeated, deliberate lease violations with no legitimate purpose
choice_c: Refused to pay any rent for several consecutive months without justification
choice_d: Damaged the unit intentionally and refused to allow repairs
explanation: Section 83.64, F.S., protects a tenant who, in good faith, has complained to a governmental agency charged with enforcing building, housing, or health codes about a suspected violation -- retaliating against the tenant for making such a complaint is prohibited.
source_note: Section 83.64, F.S. (retaliatory conduct -- protected activity: code complaints)

question: Under Section 83.64, F.S., even where a tenant has engaged in a legally protected activity, a landlord retains the ability to pursue eviction where the landlord has:
choice_a: Good cause for the eviction, such as nonpayment of rent or a genuine lease violation
choice_b: No cause of any kind, since protected activity always bars eviction permanently
choice_c: Only a personal preference for a different tenant, with no other justification
choice_d: A desire to raise the rent above market rate for the same protected tenant
explanation: Section 83.64, F.S., does not immunize a tenant from eviction merely because the tenant previously engaged in protected activity; a landlord retains the right to pursue eviction for good cause -- such as nonpayment of rent or a genuine, unrelated lease violation -- so long as retaliation is not the primary motivation.
source_note: Section 83.64, F.S. (retaliatory conduct -- landlord's good-cause defense)

question: Under Section 83.48, F.S., in a civil action to enforce a residential rental agreement or Chapter 83, Part II, F.S., the prevailing party is generally entitled to recover from the nonprevailing party:
choice_a: Reasonable attorney's fees and court costs
choice_b: Triple the amount in controversy automatically, in every case
choice_c: Nothing; each party always bears its own fees and costs regardless of outcome
choice_d: Only court costs, with attorney's fees categorically unrecoverable
explanation: Section 83.48, F.S., provides that in a civil action brought to enforce the rental agreement or the provisions of Chapter 83, Part II, F.S., the party in whose favor judgment is rendered may recover reasonable attorney's fees and court costs from the nonprevailing party.
source_note: Section 83.48, F.S. (attorney's fees and costs -- prevailing party)

question: Under Section 83.48, F.S., a residential lease provision purporting to waive a party's statutory right to recover attorney's fees under that section is:
choice_a: Unenforceable, since the right to attorney's fees under Section 83.48, F.S., may not be waived in a lease agreement
choice_b: Fully enforceable as written, since parties may waive any statutory right by contract
choice_c: Enforceable only if the tenant is represented by counsel at signing
choice_d: Enforceable only against the landlord, never against the tenant
explanation: Section 83.48, F.S., expressly provides that the right to attorney's fees under that section may not be waived in a lease agreement, preventing landlords from drafting around the statute's fee-shifting protection for either party.
source_note: Section 83.48, F.S. (attorney's fees right may not be waived in the lease)

question: Under Section 83.60, F.S., a tenant who wishes to raise a defense other than payment in a residential eviction (unlawful detainer) action generally must, within 5 days after service of process:
choice_a: Pay into the court registry the accrued rent alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court
choice_b: Simply file a written denial with no payment obligation of any kind
choice_c: Pay the full remaining balance of the entire lease term into the court registry
choice_d: Pay nothing, since Florida law never requires a rent deposit to raise a defense
explanation: Section 83.60(2), F.S., requires a tenant who wishes to raise defenses other than payment in an eviction action to deposit the accrued rent, as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court, into the court registry within 5 days after service of process.
source_note: Section 83.60(2), F.S. (rent deposit requirement to preserve eviction defenses)

question: Under Section 83.60, F.S., a tenant who fails to timely deposit the required accrued rent into the court registry to preserve eviction defenses generally:
choice_a: Waives all defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal
choice_b: Suffers no consequence, since the deposit requirement is merely optional guidance
choice_c: Automatically wins the eviction case regardless of the missed deadline
choice_d: Is entitled to an automatic 90-day extension to comply
explanation: Section 83.60(2), F.S., provides that a tenant's failure to timely deposit the required rent into the court registry constitutes an absolute waiver of all defenses other than payment, entitling the landlord to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant.
source_note: Section 83.60(2), F.S. (consequence of failing to timely deposit rent)

question: Under Section 83.60, F.S., a tenant residing in public or subsidized housing who must deposit rent into the court registry to preserve eviction defenses generally must deposit:
choice_a: Only that portion of the full rent for which the tenant is personally responsible under the assistance program
choice_b: The full, unsubsidized market rent, regardless of the subsidy arrangement
choice_c: Nothing at all, since subsidized tenants are entirely exempt from this requirement
choice_d: Double the tenant's normal rent share as a penalty
explanation: Section 83.60(2), F.S., recognizes that public housing tenants or tenants receiving rent subsidies are required to deposit into the court registry only that portion of the full rent for which they are personally responsible under their assistance program, not the full unsubsidized rent amount.
source_note: Section 83.60(2), F.S. (reduced deposit for subsidized-housing tenants)
